summary:
Lesotho does not criminalise same-sex conduct. The common-law crime of sodomy was struck down in 2012, the US State Department's 2016 human rights report for Lesotho records no criminalisation, and a joint stakeholder report to the Universal Periodic Review filed in October 2024 by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho likewise confirms that same-sex conduct is lawful while noting that no anti-discrimination protections exist.

There is no legal gender recognition in Lesotho. No statute permits a change of the gender marker on official documents. A 2017 constitutional analysis by the Southern African Litigation Centre sets out the absence of any statutory route, and a October 2020 briefing by the same organisation with the People's Matrix Association and the Women and Law in Southern Africa Research and Education Project, 'Legal Gender Recognition in Lesotho', assesses the country's law and policy against international best practice and finds no framework meeting it.

For a trans traveller the document problem is immediate. On the 2017 assessment, a person travelling on a passport whose marker does not match their presentation or stated identity could face a charge, because no statutory procedure exists to have the document recognised as consistent with the holder's gender.

The constitutional position remains an argument rather than enacted law. The 2017 analysis concludes that section 4(1) of the Constitution, through the grounds of sex and other status, should be read to cover gender identity on the authority of the UN Human Rights Committee. That interpretation has not been written into statute, and it has not been shown to have been applied by a court.

Violence and service exclusion are documented. The October 2024 joint UPR report records discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people in Lesotho, community-level discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and expression and sex characteristics, and barriers to health and education services. The 2016 US State Department report separately documents societal stigma against LGBT people. Protection machinery is thin: the International Commission of Jurists' November 2024 UPR submission raised LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination as one of three key concerns for Lesotho.

Employment sits under the Labour Act 2024, which sets the current statutory framework covering unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, and forced and child labour prohibitions. The 2017 analysis records that the Labour Code's non-discrimination clause omitted gender and sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
The People's Matrix Association is recorded in the October 2020 briefing as the only known LGBTI organisation in Lesotho, which means support infrastructure for a visitor who runs into trouble is limited to a small number of community bodies, including the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho and the Women and Law in Southern Africa Research and Education Project.

The constitutional route is live even though it is unenacted. Section 4(1) provides grounds of sex and other status, and the 2017 reading derived from the UN Human Rights Committee gives a trans litigant an argument to advance, so exposure on documents is not the same as a settled statutory prohibition.

Lesotho's human rights record is under active international scrutiny, with UPR submissions filed by the joint stakeholder coalition in October 2024 and by the International Commission of Jurists in November 2024. This signals an open channel for complaints but no domestic remedy has been shown to follow from it.

Barriers to health services reported in the October 2024 stakeholder report affect a traveller who needs care, since stigma at the point of service is documented rather than hypothetical.
localsOnly:
Residents have statutory workplace rights under the Labour Act 2024, which addresses unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, and prohibitions on forced and child labour. Whether the Act's unfair discrimination provision expressly covers gender identity and sexual orientation is not stated in the sources held.

Residents seeking to change a gender marker on an identity document or birth record have no statutory mechanism to use. The only route argued in the sources is constitutional, through section 4(1) on the grounds of sex and other status, an interpretation advanced in the 2017 Southern African Litigation Centre analysis and not enacted.

Community organisations available to residents include the People's Matrix Association, the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho and the Women and Law in Southern Africa Research and Education Project, which conducted community consultations for the 2020 gender recognition briefing.

The October 2024 stakeholder report records community-level discrimination and barriers to health and education services as everyday conditions for LGBT Basotho, alongside rape and assault, so the practical burden falls on residents rather than visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa requirements for trans travellers, including any screening of passport markers at border or airport, are not covered by the sources held, and no immigration rule on document presentation has been located.

Whether the Labour Act 2024's unfair discrimination clause names gender identity, gender expression or sexual orientation is unresolved on the material available; the sources give the Act's subject matter but not its protected-grounds list.

No hate-crime statute or aggravated-penalty provision addressing anti-trans or anti-LGBT violence is sourced for Lesotho, so the question of enhanced penalties for the assaults documented in the October 2024 report stays open.

The 2017 conclusion that a trans traveller could be charged over a non-matching passport is a legal analysis; no reported arrest, prosecution or judicial decision applying it has been found in the inventory.
